title: Feature switches without permission confusion
description: Understand what frontend flags expose, how grouped switches interact and why backend readiness still matters.

chapters.title: Visibility is one part of availability

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine a fictional administrator enabling a new Hub feature. A switch makes its menu appear. Does that mean everybody can use it and all its services are running?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No. Frontend feature flags expose pages, controls and optional data sources. They don't grant permissions or start backend services. Treat visibility, authorization and service readiness as three separate questions.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So a hidden button isn't proof that an account lacks permission, and a visible one isn't a permission grant?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. Look at the documented flag and the existing access rules together. The guide maps deployment values to frontend settings so you can explain what a switch actually changes.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Our administrator enables a project control, but it still doesn't appear. Could a bigger switch be overriding it?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes. Organisation and project controls have a hierarchy. An explicitly set organisation umbrella can govern the whole family. When group switches are unset, child settings can act independently according to the documented rules.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So empty, off and on aren't always interchangeable?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Correct. An empty group setting can mean let the more specific choices apply. Read the hierarchy before flipping several settings at once. The organisation and project guide also separates the visible working context from actual authorization.

chapters.title: Expose only what the deployment supports

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What about adding another live transport to the selector?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The frontend flag can expose the choice, but the transport may also need a compatible Agent, relay or other connection configuration. Likewise, showing remote recording controls doesn't override the Agent's capability or the user's permission.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And editing and redaction have their own combination of switches?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Yes. Related controls can depend on an umbrella and a child feature, while the rendering worker is a separate backend requirement. A switch can reveal the doorway without installing the room behind it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How should the administrator make a reliable change?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use the guide's current Helm values and documented value types, apply the change through the deployment process, then verify the actual frontend runtime settings and user experience. Don't assume every setting has identical chart exposure.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's the final check before telling the team a feature is ready?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Confirm the control is visible to the intended user, the user is authorized, and the required service works end to end. Those three checks prevent a configuration change from turning into an accidental promise of a feature the deployment cannot deliver.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses such as 'Oh, that makes sense' or 'Wait, so...' followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one or two light reactions such as 'Ha, fair point.' Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. These are spoken reactions, not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity, surprise, and emphasis. Avoid all-caps shouting, excessive exclamation marks, and artificial pause tags.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never mock the listener, joke about real victims, minimize security or data-loss risks, or let humour replace an explanation. Personality is optional; accuracy and clarity are not.
